ta-l1d37q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus (accessus) mapping the structure of Peter Lombard's text at this point in the Sentences: having shown how things are in God, Lombard now shows, by contrast, how God is in things. The paragraph traces Lombard's own division into the fact that God is everywhere and in all things, the removal from God of properties that follow upon creatures existing in place, the modes by which God is said to be in things, the confirmation of those modes by authorities, and the reasons underlying them. It closes by identifying the two questions this quaestio will actually investigate: whether God is in all things, and the diversity of the modes by which he is said to be in things.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e143.summary: First objection against God being in things. Among the causes of a thing, only those that are intrinsic parts of it (matter and form) are properly said to be 'in' it, not agent and end causes. God is not a cause of things as entering into their constitution, since (per the Liber de causis) he governs all things without being mixed with them. Therefore God is not in created things.
claims: Only causes that are intrinsic parts of a thing (matter and form) are properly said to be in that thing.
God governs things without being mixed with them and so is not in creatures.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e146.summary: Second objection. A more noble agent is one that can produce its effect while absent, rather than one that must be present to act. Since God is the most noble agent, and since even lesser agents (the sun heating the earth, a king ruling through his command) act at a distance, God a fortiori should be able to produce his effects while absent from the things he creates, so that his presence within things is not required.
claims: An agent capable of producing an effect in its own absence is more noble than one requiring presence.
As the most noble agent, God can produce effects while absent from creatures, so need not be in them.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e149.summary: Third objection. The more noble an agent, the more noble the effect it can produce. It is more perfect for an effect to persist in being once its cause is removed (as a seal's impression remains in wax after the seal is withdrawn) than for it to require the cause's continued presence (as a figure disappears in water). Since God is the most perfect agent, he should have endowed things with the ability to be conserved in existence even without his continued presence, so that his presence is not needed for the conservation of things.
claims: A more perfect agent produces effects capable of persisting after the cause is withdrawn.
God, as most perfect agent, would grant creatures the ability to persist in being without his continued presence.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e153.summary: Fourth objection. Two agents cannot immediately and perfectly operate the very same effect at once, since a single operation proceeding from a single agent terminates in a single effect. But (per John Damascene) each thing has its own proper operation by which it produces its own effects. It follows that God is not the immediate operator of whatever occurs in things, and therefore is not in all things.
claims: A single operation from a single agent cannot be duplicated immediately by another agent on the same effect.
Since created things have their own proper operations, God cannot be the immediate operator in all things.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e156.summary: Fifth objection. Demons are among the things that exist. But it is most absurd to say that God is in demons. Therefore God is not in all things.
claims: It would be absurd to say God is in demons.
Therefore God cannot be in all existing things without qualification.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e159.summary: First argument for the opposing position (sed contra), drawn from Jeremiah 23:24, 'Do I not fill heaven and earth?' Since 'heaven and earth' signifies every creature (as is clear from the opening of Genesis), the text concludes that God is in every creature.
claims: Scripture (Jer. 23:24) affirms that God fills heaven and earth, i.e. every creature, and so is in all creatures.
concepts: heaven and earth as totality of creation

ta-l1d37q1-d1e165.summary: Second sed contra argument, from Hebrews 1:3, 'bearing all things by the word of his power.' Since a cause cannot conserve things it is not present to, this text likewise implies that God is present in all things.
claims: Scripture (Heb. 1:3) implies God's conservation of all things requires his presence to them, hence he is in all things.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e171.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 1: God is essentially in all things, though not as a part mixed into their constitution. Thomas establishes this through three preliminary points. First, mover and moved must be together, but this holds differently for bodies, which must be joined by contact because their essence is limited by quantity and place, and for spiritual substances, which, lacking quantity and place, are wherever what they move is (as the soul is in the body, or the mover of the heavens is where the motion begins). Second, the esse of any thing and of each of its parts is immediately from God, since according to faith only God creates, and to create is to give being. Third, whatever is the cause of a thing's esse cannot cease its operation without the thing itself ceasing to be — unlike a merely natural agent, which is cause only of motion or becoming (as a builder is not the sustaining cause of a house, which is rather the persisting weight of its stones), the divine agent is cause of esse itself (citing Avicenna, Gregory, and John 5:17, 'my Father worketh until now, and I work'). Thomas concludes that God is therefore most intimately present to each thing, as a thing's own esse is intimate to it, since nothing could begin or continue to exist except through God's operation conjoining it to its own act of being.
claims: God is essentially in all things, but not as a constituent part of them.
Spiritual substances, unlike bodies, are present wherever they act because they are not limited by quantity and place.
The esse of every thing is immediately and continuously caused by God, who alone creates.
God, as cause of esse rather than merely of motion or becoming, cannot cease operating in a thing without that thing ceasing to exist.
God is therefore most intimately present to every thing, as intimate to it as its own act of being.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e177.summary: Reply to the first objection. Although the divine essence is not intrinsic to a thing as a part entering into its constitution, it is nonetheless within the thing as operating and effecting the esse of each thing. Thomas notes this holds for every incorporeal agent, as was established earlier (distinction 8, question 1, article 2).
claims: Divine essence is present within a thing not as a constituent part but as the operative cause of its esse, a mode of presence proper to every incorporeal agent.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e181.summary: Reply to the second objection. An agent that acts through its absence is not a proximate cause of its effect but a remote one — the sun's power is first impressed on the body nearest it and only then transmitted further (per Avicenna); a king's command is the first, remote cause, while whoever executes it is the proximate, conjoined cause. God, however, operates immediately in all things, and so must be in all things.
claims: Agents that act through absence are remote, not proximate, causes.
Because God acts immediately in all things, he must be present in all things.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e184.summary: Reply to the third objection. The esse of a thing cannot be conserved without its cause of being, just as motion cannot occur without a moving cause. If a thing's esse were conserved without any agent, that agent would only have been the cause of its becoming (fieri), not of its being (esse) — as a seal causes the figure impressed in wax, yet the figure remains once the seal is removed. Such an agent would be imperfect, so the objection's premise (that persistence-after-withdrawal marks the more perfect effect) is false.
claims: Esse cannot persist without a continuously operating cause of esse, unlike a merely formal effect such as an impressed figure.
An agent whose effect persists after its withdrawal is a cause of fieri, not of esse, and is therefore imperfect rather than more perfect.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e187.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Two proximate causes cannot operate the same effect in the same way, but can in different ways. Thomas illustrates this with an ordered series of causes a, b, c, where c, the last, exercises the operation by its own power, which it has from b, which in turn has it from a, the first cause; tracing 'why' through the series always resolves back into the power of the first cause. Since God is the first cause of all things, his power is the most immediate of all to them; and because God is his own power (rather than merely possessing it), he is not only the immediate principle of operation in all things but is himself immediately operating in all things — a mode of causal immediacy unique to God, even though each individual thing retains its own proper operations.
claims: Distinct causes can be proximate to the same effect in different respects without contradiction.
In an ordered series of causes, the power of the first cause is present, most immediately, in the operation of the last.
Because God is identical with his own power, he is immediately operating in all things, not merely their remote principle — a mode of immediacy proper to God alone.
concepts: divine simplicity (God as his own power)

ta-l1d37q1-d1e190.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. It is not to be conceded without qualification that God is in the demon, for two reasons. First, 'demon' does not name nature alone but a deformed nature, and God is not the cause of that deformity. Second, 'demon' names an intellectual nature, so the intellectual mode proper to it — grace — is what the statement 'God is in the demon' would imply if asserted simply; hence we likewise do not say without qualification that God is in a sinful man, unless it is added that this holds insofar as he is a creature, or through essence, presence, and power — with that qualification, God can also be said to be in the demon.
claims: 'Demon' signifies a deformed, not merely natural, intellectual nature, so unqualified statements about God's indwelling do not apply to it as they would to nature simply.
God can rightly be said to be in the demon only in the qualified sense proper to every creature (through essence, presence, and power), not in the sense proper to intellectual creatures (grace).

ta-l1d37q1-d1e202.summary: First objection of Article 2, against distinguishing several modes of God's being in things. To say God is in things signifies how God relates to things. But (per Dionysius) God relates to all things in one way, even though not all things relate to him in the same way. It seems, therefore, that there should be only a single mode of God existing in things, not several.
claims: Since God relates to all things uniformly, there should be only one mode of his being in things, not several.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e205.summary: Continuation of the first objection, anticipating and rebutting the response that the modes diversify according to the creature's differing relations to God. Against this: every single effect God produces in a creature causes some relation of that creature to God. But God's effects in creatures are practically infinite. It would follow that God should be said to be in creatures in infinitely many modes, not merely five.
claims: If modes of divine indwelling tracked every creaturely relation caused by a divine effect, there would be infinitely many such modes, not the traditional five.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e208.summary: Third objection, further pressing the difficulty. The relations according to which creatures diversely relate to God are not found equally in all creatures, yet some of the traditional modes — namely by essence, presence, and power — belong to every creature alike. It seems, therefore, that these modes cannot after all be distinguished on the basis of the creature's varying relation to God.
claims: Because essence, presence, and power belong equally to every creature, these modes cannot be grounded in the creature's varying relation to God.
concepts: essence, presence, and power as universal modes

ta-l1d37q1-d1e212.summary: Continuation of the objection, anticipating the reply that the modes are distinguished instead according to different divine attributes. Against this: power does not differ from essence any more than knowledge and will differ from each other. Yet being-in-things by essence and by power are treated as two distinct modes. It should follow, by parity of reasoning, that the modes would multiply according to every divine attribute, not remain at a fixed small number.
claims: If modes were distinguished by differing divine attributes, they should multiply with every attribute (e.g. knowledge, will), not remain limited to the traditional set.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e215.summary: Sed contra: the position is affirmed simply by appeal to what is stated in the text (littera) under discussion and confirmed there by authorities, without independent argument being offered in this article.
claims: The traditional distinction of modes is upheld on the authority of the text and the authorities it cites.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e218.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 2. The distinction among the modes of divine indwelling is drawn partly from the side of the creature and partly from the side of God. From the creature's side, insofar as the creature is diversely ordered to and conjoined with God — really, not merely notionally — since God is said to be in things according to how he is applied to them, a diverse mode of conjunction yields a diverse mode of indwelling. The creature is conjoined to God in three ways: first, by likeness alone, insofar as some likeness of divine goodness is found in the creature without attaining God's own substance — this is common to every creature and grounds the mode by essence, presence, and power; second, the creature attains God himself according to his substance, not merely by likeness, through operation — as when someone adheres by faith to the first truth and by charity to the highest goodness — grounding the special mode found in the saints, by grace; third, the creature attains God not only through operation but through esse itself, not as esse is the act of the divine essence (since a creature cannot pass into the divine nature) but as esse is the act of a hypostasis or person into whose union the creature is assumed — grounding the final, unique mode found in Christ, by union. From God's side, there is no real diversity but only a distinction of reason, corresponding to essence, power (virtus), and operation as distinguished in him: since the divine essence, being absolute and separate from every creature, is in a creature only insofar as it is applied through operation, God is said to be present according to how he operates in a thing; and because operation does not depart from the divine power from which it proceeds, he is said to be in a thing by power; and because that power is the divine essence itself, it follows that he is also in the thing by essence.
claims: The modes of divine indwelling are distinguished partly by the creature's real, diverse conjunction to God and partly by a merely rational distinction on God's side (essence, power, operation).

Creatures are conjoined to God in three ascending ways: by likeness alone (common to all creatures, grounding essence/presence/power), by operation attaining God's substance through faith and charity (grounding grace, proper to the saints), and by esse itself as act of a person (grounding hypostatic union, proper to Christ alone).
On God's side, presence by operation, power, and essence are really identical, distinguished only according to reason.
concepts: distinction of reason vs. real distinction

ta-l1d37q1-d1e221.summary: Reply to the first objection. Considered strictly in reality, God does relate to things in a single way; but because things relate to him in diverse ways, God comes to be signified as related diversely to things, insofar as the relations founded in creatures leave behind, in God, diverse relations according to reason. If, however, unity and distinction are considered according to reason alone, then God does relate to things in several ways — as knowing, as powerful, and so on.
claims: God's relation to things is really single but rationally multiple, since creaturely relations founded in creatures are mirrored as diverse relations of reason predicated of God.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e224.summary: Reply to the second objection. Essential division always proceeds through differences that per se divide some common genus, as 'having feet' is per se divided into biped and quadruped, not into white and black. Likewise, God's being in creatures is per se divided according to the diverse modes by which creatures attain him — an essential, formal division into a fixed, small number of modes. But if one instead considers the diverse effects found per se in creatures through which God is present only through natural effects, only a single mode of attaining God is found there; so no further division arises except one that is merely per accidens and material, which every proper art sets aside.
claims: The threefold (or fivefold) division of modes is an essential, formal division grounded in the diverse ways creatures attain God, not in the sheer multiplicity of divine effects.
Diverse natural effects considered per se yield only a per accidens, material multiplicity, not a further essential division of modes.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e227.summary: Reply to the third objection. The three modes (essence/presence/power, grace, union) are not derived from diversity in the creature but from the side of God himself operating in things, and therefore they accompany every creature and are presupposed in the other modes: wherever God is present by union, he is also present by grace, and wherever present by grace, he is also present by essence, presence, and power.
claims: The modes essence/presence/power, grace, and union are nested and cumulative: union presupposes grace, and grace presupposes essence, presence, and power.

ta-l1d37q1-d1e231.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Divine attributes are considered only according to a threefold order toward things — by operation, by power, or by essence — so there are only three modes of God's being in things (not one per attribute), corresponding to this threefold order of comparison of God to things.
claims: Divine attributes reduce, for purposes of God's relation to creatures, to a threefold order (operation, power, essence), which grounds exactly three modes of indwelling rather than one per attribute.

ta-l1d37q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium to Quaestio 1, consisting of a single divisio-textus paragraph that maps out the structure of Peter Lombard's text on God's indwelling in creatures and identifies the two questions this quaestio will pursue: whether God is in all things, and the diversity of modes by which God is said to be in things.

ta-l1d37q1-Dd1e135.summary: Article 1 asks whether God is in things at all. Five objections deny it: God is not an intrinsic constituent cause of things (per the Liber de causis); a nobler agent can act in absence, and God is most noble; a more perfect agent grants effects that persist without its presence; two agents cannot immediately produce the same effect, and creatures have their own proper operations; and it would be absurd to say God is in demons. Two scriptural sed contra arguments (Jer. 23:24 and Heb. 1:3) affirm God's presence in all things. In the respondeo, Thomas establishes, through three preliminary points about the presence of movers, the immediacy of creation, and God's status as cause of esse rather than merely of motion, that God is essentially and intimately present in every thing as the continuous cause of its very being. The replies answer each objection in turn: God is present as operative cause of esse rather than as constituent part; agents that act 'in absence' are only remote, not proximate, causes, while God acts immediately; an effect's persistence after its cause's withdrawal marks an imperfect (merely formal) cause, not a superior one; distinct causes can be proximate to the same effect in different respects, and God, being his own power, is uniquely and immediately operative in all things even though creatures retain their proper operations; and God's presence in the demon must be understood only in the qualified sense proper to every creature (essence, presence, power), not in the sense proper to intellectual creatures (grace).
claims: God is essentially present in all things as the immediate and continuous cause of their esse, not as a constituent part or a remote agent.
This immediacy distinguishes divine causality from every other agent, natural or spiritual, while leaving each creature's proper operations intact.

ta-l1d37q1-Dd1e194.summary: Article 2 asks whether God is in things by the several traditional modes — in all things by power, presence, and essence; in the saints by grace; in Christ by esse (union). Four objections argue that a plurality of modes is inconvenient: God relates to all things uniformly, so there should be one mode, not several; if modes tracked creaturely relations they would multiply to infinity given God's countless effects; essence, presence, and power belong to every creature alike, undermining a distinction grounded in creaturely diversity; and if modes tracked divine attributes they should multiply with every attribute, not stay fixed. The sed contra rests on the authority of the text. In the respondeo, Thomas grounds the distinction partly in the creature (three ascending ways of being conjoined to God — by likeness alone, by operation reaching God's substance through faith and charity, and by esse as act of the assumed person in Christ) and partly in God (a merely rational, not real, distinction among essence, power, and operation). The replies clarify that God's relation to things is really one but rationally many; that the division into modes is essential and formal, grounded in how creatures attain God, not in the sheer number of divine effects; that the three basic modes are cumulative and nested rather than mutually exclusive; and that divine attributes reduce, for this purpose, to a threefold order (operation, power, essence) that grounds exactly the traditional modes.
claims: The plurality of modes of divine indwelling is grounded in the creature's diverse and real conjunction to God (by likeness, by operation, by esse), while on God's side it reflects only a distinction of reason among essence, power, and operation.
The modes are cumulative: union presupposes grace, and grace presupposes essence, presence, and power.

ta-l1d37q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Distinction 37 investigates how God is in things, complementing the preceding discussion of how things are in God. It divides into a Prooemium locating the question within Lombard's text, and two articles. Article 1 establishes, against objections drawn from causal theory and the seeming absurdity of God's presence in demons, that God is essentially and immediately present in every created thing as the continuous cause of its esse — a presence more intimate than any other kind of causal proximity, since God, unlike any natural or created agent, is cause of being itself rather than merely of motion or becoming. Article 2 then distinguishes the modes of that presence: a common mode of essence, presence, and power found in every creature by likeness to divine goodness; a special mode of grace found in the saints through operations of faith and charity that attain God's own substance; and a unique mode of union found in Christ alone, in whom a created nature attains God through the very act of personal esse. These modes are shown to be really grounded in the creature's diverse and cumulative conjunction to God, while corresponding on God's side only to a rational, not real, distinction among essence, power, and operation.
claims: God is essentially and immediately present in every creature as the continuous cause of its esse.

The modes by which God is present — common (essence/presence/power), special (grace), and unique (union) — are really grounded in the creature's cumulative conjunction to God, and reflect on God's side only a distinction of reason.
